en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, Nissaggiyakaṇḍa (The Chapter on Forfeiture for Nuns)
The Chapter on Pairs, 8.
The Training Rule on Causing a Prostitute to Be Paid.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunīs living in the monastery quarters of a certain guild were suffering from a lack of rice gruel.
So that guild collected subscriptions for the sake of the bhikkhunīs' gruel, deposited the funds with a certain shopkeeper, and approached the bhikkhunīs, saying:
"Venerable ladies, the funds for rice gruel have been deposited with such-and-such a shopkeeper. Having had rice brought from there and having had the gruel cooked, please enjoy it."
The bhikkhunīs, having had medicine purchased with that communal requisite, used it.
When the group learned of this, they complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can the bhikkhunīs exchange one thing for another with a communal requisite intended for a specific purpose? ... [as before] ...
“Is it true, monks, that nuns are exchanging one communal requisite, intended for a specific purpose, for another?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...
"How indeed, monks, could bhikkhunīs exchange for something else an article belonging to a group, intended for a specific purpose and designated for that purpose?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of the faith of those who have it...

And thus, monks, should the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule: "Whatever bhikkhunī should exchange for something else an article belonging to a group, intended for a specific purpose and designated for that purpose, there is an offense of expiation."* (*The full rule includes the penalty clause.)

“Whatever nun, however, should have another item exchanged for a communal requisite that was intended for a specific purpose and designated for a specific use, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Regarding the phrase “whatever nun”: whoever she may be... [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"With an article intended for another purpose, dedicated to another" means:
By means of what was given for the sake of another.
"For the common people" means for a group, not for the Saṅgha, nor for a single bhikkhunī.
"Should she exchange for something else" means:
setting aside that which was given for a specific purpose, if she exchanges it for something else, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of undertaking;
with the acquisition [of the item], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It is to be relinquished to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to a single bhikkhunī.
And thus, monks, it is to be relinquished:
…pe…

“Venerable ladies, this object, which was obtained by me through an item intended for another purpose, designated for another, and belonging to a group, is to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
…pe… “She should give it,” …pe… “They should give it,” …pe…
“I give it to the noble lady.
If she exchanges something else for what was intended for another purpose, while perceiving it as being for another purpose, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she exchanges something else for what was intended for another purpose, while being in doubt, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she exchanges something for something else while perceiving it as not being for another purpose, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Having forfeited it, it must be restored to the person from whom it was received.
If she exchanges something for something else while perceiving it as being for another purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not for another’s purpose, but she is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not for another’s purpose and she perceives it as not being for another’s purpose, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
He brings it;
he brings it after having informed the owner;
in times of distress.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of a first-offender.
The eighth training rule is concluded.
